patches.value: Using the basis proved in S001, define E_ab by E_ab(e_b)=e_a and E_ab(e_t)=0 for t!=b. The divided-power formulas give Y_lambda X_lambda=E_lambda,lambda: X_lambda kills e_i for i<lambda and sends e_lambda to e_0, while Y_lambda sends e_0 to e_lambda. They also give X_(lambda-i)E_lambda,lambda=E_i,lambda, since X_(lambda-i)e_lambda=e_i, and E_lambda,lambda Y_(lambda-j)=binom(lambda,j)E_lambda,j. Indeed, for an input e_k with k<j, the divided-power formula gives Y_(lambda-j)e_k=binom(k+lambda-j,lambda-j)e_(k+lambda-j), which is generally nonzero but has index less than lambda and is killed by E_lambda,lambda; for k=j it gives binom(lambda,j)e_lambda; and for k>j the Y-string has passed its endpoint, so Y_(lambda-j)e_k=0. Thus the stated identity is for the composite, not a claim that Y_(lambda-j) itself vanishes on every other basis vector. Since 0<=j<=lambda<p, neither lambda! nor j!(lambda-j)! is divisible by p, so binom(lambda,j) is a unit in R=Z_(p); this includes lambda=0 (the empty factorial is 1) and p=2. Therefore every E_i,j belongs to the R-algebra generated by the divided powers and preserves M_R.
